'''''Potamogeton trichoides''''' is a species of [[aquatic plant]] known by the common name '''hairlike pondweed''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref> native to Europe and western Asia where it grows in calcareous, usually nutrient-rich standing or slow-flowing water.

==Description==
Hairlike pondweed is an aquatic perennial that dies back each winter into a large number of asexually produced resting bodies called [[Turion (botany)|turions]]. There are no rhizomes. It produces slender, cylindrical or slightly compressed,  branching stems usually less than a metre in length but occasionally up to 2 m.<ref name='Preston'/> The submerged leaves are long and very narrow, typically 16–80 mm long and 0.3–1 mm wide, with the midrib occupying up to 70% of the width of the leaf near the base.<ref name='Preston'/> They are rigid and green turning darker with age. There are no floating leaves.<ref name='Preston'/>

The [[inflorescence]] is a short spike of 3–5 flowers arising from the water on a slender [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]].

This species readily [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridizes]] with several other species of ''[[Potamogeton]]'' including [[Potamogeton berchtoldii|''P. berchtoldii'']] (''P.'' × ''franconicus'' <small>G.Fisch.</small>), [[Potamogeton pusillus|''P. pusillus'']] (''P.'' × ''grovesii'' <small>Dandy & G.Taylor</small>) and [[Potamogeton compressus|''P. compressus'']] (''P.'' × ''ripoides'' <small>Baagøe</small>).<ref name='Preston'/><ref name=kwc2/>

Hairlike pondweed is diploid, with 2n=26 [[chromosome]]s.<ref name=Kap2/>

Hairlike pondweed is one of the more distinctive fine-leaved pondweeds due to the characteristically stiff leaves dominated by the midrib and open but tightly rolled stipules. However, it tends to be rarer than other fine-leaved species and often grows in mixed beds with other fine-leaved water plants such as ''P. pusillus'' and ''Zannichellia palustris'', so it may be overlooked.

==Taxonomy==
''Potamogeton trichoides'' (trichoides = 'hairlike') was named by the German botanists [[Adelbert von Chamisso]] and [[Diederich Franz Leonhard von Schlechtendal]] in 1827.

Hairlike pondweed is one of the fine-leaved pondweed clade (series ''Graminifolii''), and related to similar species such as ''P. pusillus''.<ref name='Preston'/><ref name=Lind/>

==Distribution==
''Potamogeton trichoides'' is native to the western Palaearctic and Africa. It occurs in northern Europe (Austria, Britain,<ref name='Preston'/> Czech Republic, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy (including Sicily),  Norway, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Poland, Russia, the Baltic States), North Africa (Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt), eastern and southern Africa (South Africa, Tanzania, Uganda, Zimbabwe).<ref name=Sweden/><ref name=NewAt/><ref name=Allen/>  There are outlying populations in the Canaries, the Caucasus, and Russia east of the Urals.<ref name=Sweden/>

==Ecology and conservation==
Hairlike pondweed grows predominantly in standing water including ponds, lakes, ditches, canals and slow-flowing rivers and streams. It is usually restricted to calcareous water of rather high conductivity and is tolerant of high nutrient levels.<ref name='Preston'/> It is often an early succession species, colonising newly created habitats such as ditches and flooded gravel pits,<ref name='Preston'/> but sometimes is abundant in alkaline, low altitude lakes.<ref name=Burgess/> It often grows with other nutrient tolerant macrophytes such as ''Myriophyllum spicatum'', ''Potamogeton crispus'', ''P. pusillus'' and ''Ranunculus circinatus''.<ref name=NewAt/>

In Britain, hairlike pondweed is thought to be stable or possibly increasing.<ref name=NewAt/>  However, it is placed in various threat categories in parts of its range, for example it is Vulnerable in the Czech Republic,<ref name=Grulich/> and Germany (although still widespread along all major river systems there),<ref name=floraw/> and Critically Endangered in Switzerland.<ref name=Moser/>

==Cultivation==
''Potamogeton trichoides'' is not in general cultivation, and is of little garden merit.
